tasks.title: Package skeleton, command-line stub, requirements.txt
tasks.why_tier: One obvious right answer: names, signatures and error codes are all given in spec section 2.
tasks.brief: Create the package folder `mlprofessor` (spec 2). `mlprofessor.profile` with exactly the signature and defaults of 2.1; for now it may raise NotImplementedError. A `ProfileResult` class (2.3) to be filled later. `mlprofessor/errors.py` with every class of 2.4, each subclassing `ProfileError` and carrying its `code`. `mlprofessor/extensions.py` with the context manager `use(families=None, steps=None)` exactly as 2.6 describes (it stores the overrides, restores the previous state on exit including after an exception, and nests). An empty module `mlprofessor/stages.py` that later tasks fill. The command line of 2.2: `python -m mlprofessor profile` with every option, calling `profile`, exit codes 0, 2 and 3; `--help` must exit 0. `requirements.txt` pinning pandas==3.1.1, numpy==2.5.4, scikit-learn==1.9.1 and threadpoolctl==3.8.0. Install nothing: all four are already in the interpreter, and the package itself is never installed.

tasks.title: Load one table; count usable rows
tasks.why_tier: Carries F6: a row lost here is lost from every count that follows.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.load_table(data)` and `stages.usable_rows(frame, target, time_col=None)` (spec 2.7), implementing step 1 and step 2 of section 3 and the loading rules of section 6. Read spec section 9 first: pandas 3 renames duplicate headers silently, skips blank lines, and turns the first column into an index when rows are longer than the header. The loader reads the header line itself to catch duplicates. `row` positions are fixed here and never change.

tasks.title: Column roles that need no target
tasks.why_tier: Carries F6 and decides which columns ever reach a model.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.column_roles(frame, target, time_col=None)` (spec 2.7): the rule table of step 5, in its order, with the cut-offs of 4.3 and the date forms of 4.5. Roles are judged on the usable rows; `n_missing`, `n_coerced` and `n_infinite` are counted over every row. Whole numbers are judged by value, never by dtype (a blank cell makes an integer column float). Never use pandas' date parser to decide whether a column is a date. A number written with thousands separators (`1,200`; the pattern is pinned in step 5) is never parsed, and a column is never used with such cells left out. Rule 4a comes before the coercion rule: a column in which at least 90% of the non-missing values parse or match the pattern, and at least one matches, is excluded with the reason `numeric_with_separators`, whether it is written that way throughout or is plain numbers with a single such cell (D28, D34). A column whose text cells are of another kind (`abc`) is still read as numeric with those cells coerced, and one holding `1,200` in every row is `constant`. This function returns no warnings.

tasks.title: Task decision
tasks.why_tier: Carries F5: the wrong task puts the headline on the wrong scale.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.decide_task(values, task="auto")` (spec 2.7, step 4 of section 3). Count distinct values; ignore the type for the two-value rule. Raise the named errors rather than guess. Return the classes in sorted order with the second as the positive class, and the `whole_number_regression_target` warning code when the rule picks regression on whole numbers.

tasks.title: Random holdout and folds
tasks.why_tier: Decides which rows every number is computed on.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.split_random(n_rows, classes=None, seed=0)` (spec 2.7, step 7 of section 3, random scheme): the holdout of ceil(n/4) rows first, stratified when `classes` is given, then five folds that partition the remaining rows. Everything comes from the seed.

tasks.title: Time column, time-ordered holdout, expanding folds, gap
tasks.why_tier: Carries F7: a training row at or after the holdout, or a misread date, gives an optimistic number with no error.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.read_time(values)` and `stages.split_time(keys, gap=0)` (spec 2.7; steps 3 and 7 of section 3). `read_time` accepts exactly the three forms of step 3 and raises `TimeColumnError` for anything else; text is matched against the ISO 8601 pattern before any parsing, and day-first or month-first text is never parsed. `split_time` cuts at whole timestamps, makes six contiguous blocks as numpy.array_split would, and takes the gap off before the holdout and before every validation block.

tasks.title: Metrics, skill and the previous-value baseline
tasks.why_tier: Carries F4 and F8; exact arithmetic that every headline rests on.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.roc_auc`, `stages.mse`, `stages.skill` and `stages.previous_value` (spec 2.7; step 11 of section 3). ROC AUC by ranks with ties sharing their average rank, in numpy. Accuracy is not a metric here.

tasks.title: Preprocessing fitted on the rows it is given
tasks.why_tier: Carries F1: preprocessing that learns from the wrong rows is the small, invisible form of leakage.
tasks.brief: Build `stages.Preprocessor(kinds)` with `fit(frame)` and `transform(frame)` (spec 2.7; 'Preprocessing' under step 8 of section 3): median imputation and standardisation for numeric columns, the level `(missing)` and one-hot columns for at most the 30 most frequent levels for categorical columns. Every statistic comes from the frame given to `fit`.

tasks.title: Fit, select, score once: the run in memory, random scheme, fast profile
tasks.why_tier: Carries F1 and F3: this is where a refit on the wrong rows or a cross-validation score as the headline would happen.
tasks.brief: Make `profile()` run in memory under the random scheme with `profile="fast"`, following steps 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 and 11 of spec section 3 by calling the step functions already built: load, usable rows, task, roles, the fast profile's random row cap, `split_random`, then for each configuration and fold a fresh `Preprocessor` and model fitted on the fold's training rows, selection by `cv_mean`, one refit on all training rows, one scoring of the holdout, the baselines and skill. The two families of the fast profile are `linear-0` and `tree-0` (4.1). Honour `extensions.use` (2.6): families replace the built-in ones, steps run first, every fit gets fresh objects and DataFrames indexed by source row position. A configuration that raises is recorded as failed and never chosen; all failing raises. Hold BLAS to one thread and OpenMP to `n_jobs` with threadpoolctl for the whole run. Return a `ProfileResult` whose `predictions`, `models`, `rows`, `columns`, `warnings` and `headline` (metric, score, model, baseline, baseline_score, skill) are populated. No time column, no leak screen, no interval, no files yet.

tasks.title: profile.json, predictions.csv and the command line: the first run the gate can judge
tasks.why_tier: First task the gate judges; owns reconciliation between the source, the files and the result object.
tasks.brief: Complete the output of spec section 5 for the random scheme under the fast profile: every key of `profile.json` (5.2), with fields that later tasks fill written as null or empty (the interval and p-value fields, `limitations`); `predictions.csv` (5.1); `to_dict()`, `to_json(path)` and `out_dir`; the DataFrames equal to their JSON parts (2.3). The command line writes both files, prints a short summary, exits 3 with `error: <code>: <message>` on a named error and writes nothing then. Add the warnings that arise in steps 1 to 11: `values_coerced`, `numeric_with_separators` (one per column excluded with that reason by rule 4a of step 5; it has no other form), `infinite_values`, `blank_header`, `duplicate_rows`, `whole_number_regression_target`, `small_holdout`, `fold_not_scored`, `model_failed`. No NaN in the JSON. Only `meta.timing` may hold a clock value.

tasks.title: Time-ordered scheme wired into the run, with its baselines
tasks.why_tier: Carries F7 and F8.
tasks.brief: When `time_col` is given, follow the time-ordered path of spec section 3: read the time column (step 3), drop and count rows with no time value, apply the fast profile's cap as the most recent whole timestamps (step 6, `FastProfileError` for a wide panel), split with `split_time` (step 7), count `dropped_gap` and each fold's `gap_rows`, fill the time fields of `validation` (5.2). Regression baselines under time order (step 11): with unique timestamps score both `training_mean` and `previous_value` and use the lower error; with repeated timestamps use the training mean and raise `autocorrelated_panel_target` above 0.5. When `time_col` is not given and a column was excluded as `datetime`, raise `date_column_undeclared`. `--gap` without `--time-col` is an input error.

tasks.title: Leak screen
tasks.why_tier: Carries F2, and a screen fitted on the wrong rows is itself F1.
tasks.brief: Add the leak screen of step 8 of spec section 3, run on training rows only, before any model: the missing-by-class rule, then the single-column cross-validated skill with the pinned tree over the selection folds, cut-offs of 4.3. Under time order it uses the expanding folds and, for regression with unique timestamps, the previous-value baseline, so a lagged target on a random walk is not flagged. A flagged column is excluded with reason `suspected_leak`, its `leak_rule` and a warning, and reaches no model. The same skill, measured once per column, also decides the warning tier (rule 3 of step 8, D30): at least 0.90 and below 0.98, the column stays a feature and a `strong_single_column` warning names it. No feature left raises `NoFeaturesError`.

tasks.title: Interval and p-value, row and block forms
tasks.why_tier: Decides how certain the headline looks; the resampling must respect time order.
tasks.brief: Add step 12 of spec section 3, from the holdout predictions alone, nothing refitted: the percentile bootstrap interval on score and skill and the permutation p-value under the random scheme; the moving-block bootstrap over distinct holdout timestamps under time order, with the p-value absent and its reason given; no interval below 30 holdout timestamps, with a reason and the `no_interval` warning. Whenever the interval does come from the block bootstrap, add exactly one `interval_approximate` warning with a null column (D27); never under the random scheme. 200 resamples under fast, 1,000 under full. Fill the interval and p-value fields of `headline` (5.2).

tasks.title: Random forest and histogram gradient boosting behind the existing family interface
tasks.why_tier: One concern behind an interface that already exists; the estimators and their arguments are given in spec 4.1.
tasks.brief: Under `profile="full"` run three families in the order linear, forest, boosting (spec 4.1), each with at least its index-0 configuration, for both tasks, through the same family interface the fast profile uses. Forests are fitted with `n_jobs` and predict on one thread. The regression forest's default `max_features` is one third. Keep the handling of a configuration that raises: status `failed`, error text, `model_failed` warning, never chosen; every configuration failing raises `AllModelsFailedError`.

tasks.title: The full profile's grids, and the same result at any n_jobs
tasks.why_tier: Carries F3: with 18 configurations the best cross-validation score is optimistic, and selection must not touch the holdout.
tasks.brief: Complete the grids of spec 4.1: exactly 18 configurations under `full`, named and ordered as given, `params` holding the grid arguments. Selection over all of them by `cv_mean` with ties to the earlier family then the earlier grid position; only the chosen one is refitted and scored on the holdout. `meta.n_jobs` records the cores used. The same seed must give identical files at any `n_jobs` (D17): BLAS on one thread always, OpenMP on `n_jobs`, forests predicting on one thread.

tasks.title: Edges, limitations statement, console summary
tasks.why_tier: A clear contract: every edge, code and fixed text is listed in the spec.
tasks.brief: Walk the table of spec section 7 row by row and make each edge give its named error or its reported outcome; none may be skipped silently. Every invalid argument of 2.1 raises `InputError`. Write the fixed limitations statement (nine strings) and the random-split caveat of 5.4 exactly. Make the console summary short and plain: task, scheme, row counts, skill with its metric, baseline and interval, the p-value when there is one, and each warning.

tasks.title: README with run instructions
tasks.why_tier: Prose from known facts.
tasks.brief: Write `README.md` for a data scientist: what the tool measures and what it does not (the limitations of spec 5.4, in plain words), how to call `mlprofessor.profile` and the command line with the interpreter at E:\CODE\ml-professor\mlprof_env\Scripts\python.exe from the repo root, what `profile.json` and `predictions.csv` contain, the two validation schemes and when to pass `time_col`, the fast profile. State that the package is run from the repo root and is not installed. Every command shown must work as written.

tasks.title: Guards for the first review's test holes, and two CSV edges: no code change expected
tasks.why_tier: Nothing is built here. But if a guard fails, the fix is in the code that decides which rows a fitted step sees, the most delicate code in the package.
tasks.brief: NO CODE CHANGE IS EXPECTED. These four test files guard behaviour the application already has: every test in them was measured to pass against the application on 2026-11-17, before this task existed (plan/test-plan.md, 'Second pass'). Run them first. If they all pass, change nothing and finish. If one fails, THE APPLICATION IS WRONG, NOT THE TEST: the tests are locked, and each guard was proved by running it against a copy of the reference implementation that carries exactly the fault it is named for (spec 8.1), or against the reference as it was before the decision the test holds (D42). Fix only what the failing test names, and say in your final message what you found. What each file guards: `test_guard_final_fit.py`, that the statistics of the final fit's imputation and scaling come from training rows only (M1), that one-hot levels come from the rows of each fit only (M2), and that a categorical level is the cell's text without the white space round it, in counting, in the leak screen, in what a step receives and in the matrix (D42; spec step 5); `test_guard_leak_screen.py`, that the leak screen's trees are fitted on each fold's training rows only and its missing-by-class rule counts training rows only (M3); `test_guard_uncertainty.py`, that the block bootstrap draws whole blocks of consecutive timestamps (M4) and that a shuffle whose skill equals the observed skill counts in the p-value (M5); `test_csv_edges.py`, that a file which is not valid UTF-8 is an `input_error` wherever the bad byte sits, that leading lines of only spaces and tabs are skipped when the header is read, as pandas skips them, and that a header cell holding only white space is a name like any other, so that two alike stop the run with `duplicate_columns` (D42; spec 6). These tests join the checks every later task must keep green.

tasks.title: Skill when a baseline's error is zero
tasks.why_tier: Decides which resamples the interval on skill is computed from, and what the headline reports where it has no value.
tasks.brief: When a baseline's squared error on the rows being scored is exactly zero, skill = 1 - error / baseline error has no value, and today the run dies with a ZeroDivisionError and writes nothing (D36). Make it report instead, everywhere skill is computed. (1) The headline, spec step 11: `headline.skill` is null, never an error, an infinity or a zero in its place; exactly one `skill_undefined` warning with a null column says why; the score, every baseline with its score (the zero included) and the rest of the output are reported as usual. (2) The interval, spec step 12: a resample whose baseline error is zero keeps its place in the interval on the score and is left out of the interval on skill only. Count the resamples kept for skill in a new key, `headline.n_resamples_skill_used`; `n_resamples_used` goes on counting those in which the score could be computed. If fewer than half of the resamples can be used for skill, `skill_low` and `skill_high` are null while the interval on the score stands (D40). That is always so when `headline.skill` is null, and the `skill_undefined` warning of (1) covers it: add no other. When `headline.skill` is a number and its interval cannot be computed, add exactly one warning with the code `no_skill_interval` and a null column, and no `skill_undefined` (D42): the two codes never appear together, and neither appears when there is no interval at all, which `no_interval` covers. (3) The p-value: when `headline.skill` is null, `p_value` and `n_permutations` are null and `p_value_reason` says why. (4) The leak screen, spec step 8: a column whose single-column skill cannot be computed is not flagged and gets no warning. The application already behaves so; keep it. (5) `stages.skill("mse", score, 0)` returns None (spec 2.7). (6) The command line finishes on such a table: the summary must not fail on a null skill. Schema: spec 5.2. The gate's dataset is `flat_tail`, daily sales that stop: the target is 0 from 65% of the way through the series to its end, so the previous value predicts every holdout row exactly.

tasks.title: Colliding feature names stop the run
tasks.why_tier: A clear contract in spec step 5: one check, one named error. It decides no number.
tasks.brief: The preprocessed matrix names a numeric feature by its own name and each level of a categorical feature `<column>=<level>`. Today, when two of those names are the same, one column silently overwrites the other: a numeric column named `colour=red` beside a categorical `colour` with the level `red` reaches no model and is still listed as a feature (D37). Add the named error `FeatureNameCollisionError`, code `feature_name_collision`, to `mlprofessor/errors.py`, and raise it from `profile()` as spec step 5 says ('Feature names must be distinct'): after the column roles, before the row cap, the split, the leak screen and any fit, with nothing written. The message names every column involved. Which names are compared is pinned there and is the point of this task: the columns that are features after step 5; for a categorical column EVERY level among the usable rows, not only the 30 a fit keeps, with `(missing)` when a usable row has a missing cell, a level being the cell's text without the white space round it (D42), as the application already has it; decided before the row cap, so that `fast` and `full` agree and no seed changes the outcome. A level that sits only in rows with no target does not count. Two categorical columns can collide too (`site` with the level `a=b`, beside `site=a` with the level `b`). `stages.Preprocessor.fit` raises the same error when two of the names it would give are the same, judged on the levels it keeps from the rows it is given (spec 2.7). The command line exits 3 with `error: feature_name_collision: ...`, as for any named error.

tasks.title: A configuration that fails after it is chosen
tasks.why_tier: Decides which configuration the headline comes from, and must not let the holdout take part in the choice.
tasks.brief: Spec steps 9 to 11 (D38). The application already falls back to the next best configuration by `cv_mean` when the chosen one raises on the final fit or while predicting the holdout, and already raises `all_models_failed` when none is left: keep both. What is wrong today is that the failed configuration's record is wiped: its fold scores, `cv_mean` and `cv_std` are set to null, so the models table misreports what was tried. Change that: a configuration that fails AFTER it was chosen gets status `failed`, its error text and a `model_failed` warning, and KEEPS the `fold_scores`, `cv_mean` and `cv_std` it had. A configuration that fails DURING selection is unchanged: all five fold scores null, `cv_mean` and `cv_std` null (a first-pass test pins that). The headline comes from exactly one configuration, the first in the ranking of step 9 whose refit and holdout prediction both succeed; `headline`, `cv.chosen`, `cv.chosen_mean`, the predictions, the interval and the p-value are its alone. Holdout rows are handed to one configuration at a time, in ranking order, and to none once one has predicted them. The holdout plays no part in the choice: a configuration is passed over only for raising, never for its score.

tasks.title: Small defects: the output folder, process settings, the no-features message, the console summary
tasks.why_tier: Four small contracts, each stated in spec 2.1, 2.2 or 2.4.
tasks.brief: Four defects from the first review (D39). (1) An `out_dir` that cannot be used is an `InputError` raised before anything is loaded (spec 2.1): the path, or the nearest folder above it that exists, is something other than a folder, for one when it names an existing file. Today that is an unnamed FileExistsError after the whole run. Check it with the other arguments, without creating anything. (2) Process-wide settings are left as the caller had them, whether `profile()` or a function of `stages` returns or raises (spec 2.1). The one found: the loader raises `csv.field_size_limit` for the whole process and never puts it back. Restore the caller's value in a `finally`. (3) The message of `no_features` names every excluded column and, for each, its reason as `columns[].reason` spells it (spec 2.4), both when no column is a feature after step 5 and when the leak screen removes the last one. Today it says 'see the column accounting', and an error returns none. (4) The console summary (spec 2.2) also shows: the interval on the score and the interval on skill, each end as a number, or the text of `headline.interval_reason` when there is no interval; the p-value as a number, or the text of `headline.p_value_reason` when there is none; and one line per warning holding its code and, when it has one, its column. A number counts as shown when it is printed to within 0.0005 x max(1, |value|) of the value in `profile.json`. The wording stays yours; keep it short and plain. A null skill, or a null interval on skill, needs no number: the line of its `skill_undefined` or `no_skill_interval` warning covers it.

tasks.title: The README's commands use a table kept in the repo
tasks.why_tier: Prose and three command lines, from known facts.
tasks.brief: Today every command in `README.md` reads a file under `verify/artifacts/data/`, which the project's own checks write and git ignores, so on a fresh clone no command works. The repo now holds a small example table for this purpose: `examples/customers.csv`, 400 synthetic customers, one row per sign-up date. Its columns: `customer_id` (an identifier), `signup_date` (ISO dates, year first, one row a day: usable as `--time-col`), `plan`, `region`, `monthly_spend` (six blank cells), `support_calls`, `age`, and the target `churned` (yes or no; three blank cells). Rewrite every command and the Python example in `README.md` to use it: `--data examples/customers.csv --target churned`, and for the time-ordered example `--time-col signup_date --gap 1`. After this the README names no file under `verify/` or `tests/`, in a command or anywhere else; remove the sentence that tells the reader to run the checks first. Every command shown must work as written, from the repo root, with the interpreter path already given. While you are there, bring the README's account of the output up to date with spec 2.2, 2.4 and 5.2: what the console summary now shows; that `headline.skill` can be null, with the warning `skill_undefined`, when a baseline predicts the holdout exactly, and that the warning `no_skill_interval` means skill has a value and its interval does not; the error code `feature_name_collision`. You may add a file under `examples/` only if a command needs another table, and then the README says what it is. `examples/customers.csv` itself is made by `docs/measurements/CP3/make_example.py`; leave it as it is.

tasks.title: Guard of the third pass: a line pandas reads as the header. No code change expected
tasks.why_tier: Nothing is built here. But if the guard fails, the fix is in the loader's own reading of the header line, where taking the wrong line for the header loses a column without a word.
tasks.brief: NO CODE CHANGE IS EXPECTED. `tests/test_guard_header_lines.py` guards behaviour the application already has: its one test was measured to pass against the application on 2026-11-20, in all three of its cases, before this task existed (plan/test-plan.md, 'Third pass'). Run it first. If it passes, change nothing and finish. If it fails, THE APPLICATION IS WRONG, NOT THE TEST: the test is locked, and it was proved by running it against a copy of the reference implementation whose check for long rows had been taken out (F6d, spec section 8), on which it fails. What it guards: a first line of a form feed, of a no-break space, or of two quotes round a space, before a header of two columns. pandas does not skip such a line. It reads it as a header of one column, and every line after it, the real header among them, then has more fields than the header. The loader must stop with `input_error` (spec section 6), from `stages.load_table` and from `profile()`, and write nothing. The trap: Python's `str.strip()` removes a form feed and a no-break space, and pandas skips only spaces and tabs, so a loader that picks the header line with the default `strip()` and then trusts pandas' column count reads one column and loses the other. Fix only what the failing test names, and say in your final message what you found. This test joins the checks every later task must keep green.

tasks.title: No number that is not finite is reported, or turned into null
tasks.why_tier: Decides whether a number may be reported at all, and which error the caller gets when it may not; it also changes which feature values reach a model.
tasks.brief: A regression target holding one sentinel-sized cell (1.7976931348623157e308 among values near 20), or a target on the scale of 1e160, finishes today with `score`, `baseline_score` and `skill` null, a p-value all the same, and no warning. The square of such a value is beyond the largest double, so the squared error is infinite, and `mlprofessor/result.py` turns every number that is not finite into null as the result is built (D44). Nothing may be written as null because it overflowed. Follow spec section 3, 'Numbers that are not finite', rule by rule. (1) Add the error `NonFiniteScoreError`, code `non_finite_score`, to `mlprofessor/errors.py`. (2) Score every baseline of step 11 on the holdout as soon as the split is made, before the leak screen and before any step or model is fitted. If a baseline's score is not finite, raise the new error there. Under time order with unique timestamps check both baselines. The order is the point: with a target too large for squared error the caller must get this one error, never `all_models_failed` with a list of configurations. (3) In the leak screen, for regression: if the pooled squared error of a baseline it uses (each fold's training mean; the previous value), or of the column's own tree, is not finite, raise the new error. Today a skill that is not-a-number is read as 'not flagged'. (4) During selection a configuration whose prediction is not finite is already failed: keep that. Treat a fold score that is not finite in the same way: status `failed`, an error text, a `model_failed` warning, five null fold scores, never chosen. Today such a configuration keeps the status `fitted` with a null `cv_mean`, and can still be chosen. (5) After the choice, a prediction for the holdout that is not finite already counts as raising, with the fallback of D38: keep that. If the predictions are finite and the holdout score is not, raise the new error and do NOT try the next configuration: a configuration is passed over only for raising, never for its score. (6) If the headline skill comes out not finite from a finite score and a finite baseline score, raise the new error. Skill is null only for a baseline score of exactly zero. (7) Before the result is returned or written, check that every number of `validation`, `headline`, `baselines`, `cv` and `models` is finite, and raise the new error if one is not. The conversion in `result.py` must not be what stands between a not-a-number and the output. (8) A p-value is reported only when skill is a number; with (6) and (7) that follows. (9) The message of the new error names the number: a baseline by its name as `baselines[].name` spells it (`training_mean`, `previous_value`), a configuration by its name as `models[].config` spells it, a field of the output by its key. It also gives the likely cause, such as a target value too large for squared error. (10) Three quiet fallbacks the review found, and a fourth of the same kind. None may stay as a silent default. `pipeline.py` reads a regression target with `errors="coerce"`: the target is of integer or float type there (step 4) and nothing can be coerced, so convert it plainly. `leakage.py` drops the previous-value baseline when a previous value is missing: none ever is (spec step 8, 'The previous value exists for every row it is asked for'); if one is, raise an internal error, do not fall back to the training mean. `preprocess.py` reads a deviation that is not finite as 1: with part (11) no such deviation can arise, so remove the special case and keep only 'a zero deviation is read as 1'. `pipeline.py` passes over a panel autocorrelation that is not finite: when the per-timestamp means do not vary there is no value and no warning, as now; when the number overflows, raise the new error. (11) D48: a numeric feature cell whose magnitude is above 3.4028234663852886e+38, the largest 32-bit float, is read exactly as an infinite cell is: missing, counted in `n_infinite`, named by the column's `infinite_values` warning, NaN to a step supplied through the seam, imputed in the matrix. scikit-learn's trees read 32-bit floats, and today one such cell stops the run with a raw `ValueError` from the leak screen. Apply the rule wherever a feature value is read: `stages.column_roles`, the leak screen, the feature frame, and `stages.Preprocessor` itself, in `fit` and in `transform`. A value of exactly that magnitude is kept. A target value of that size is not missing. (12) D48: a complex-number target is not numeric. `task="regression"` on it is `task_unsupported`; under `task="auto"` two distinct values are classification and anything else is `task_ambiguous`. Today it runs as a regression and loses its imaginary part. (13) From the command line a `non_finite_score` is exit 3 with exactly one line on standard error. numpy prints its overflow warnings there today: do the arithmetic that can overflow under `numpy.errstate(...)`, a context manager, so that the caller's settings are left as found (spec 2.1). Never change the warnings filters of the process. One test of this file passes today and must go on passing: `test_a_prediction_that_is_not_finite_counts_as_raising`. Where the spec leaves the outcome open (a target near 1e80, whose squared errors can be held and whose own squares cannot), either finish with finite numbers or stop with the new error: never a null, never `all_models_failed`.

tasks.title: White space round a target value; a target cell of only white space
tasks.why_tier: Decides the task, the classes, which class is positive and which rows have a target at all: every number of a classification run follows from it.
tasks.brief: D46 and D48. A text target value is read without the white space round it: `yes`, ` yes` and `yes ` are one class. Today they are three, and a yes/no target with a few trailing spaces stops with `task_ambiguous` and '4 distinct values'; written `yes ` throughout, the positive class is reported as `yes ` with its space. Make the stripped value the value everywhere the target is used (spec step 4): the count of distinct values and so the task; `task.classes` and `task.positive_class`; the 0 and 1 handed to the models; the stratification of the split; and `y_true`, in `ProfileResult.predictions` and in `predictions.csv`. Strip once, where the target is first read, so that every later step sees one value. White space is what it already is for a categorical level. `stages.decide_task` reads the values it is given in the same way, and `stages.split_random` compares text `classes` without the white space round them, so that the run's split is `split_random(n, stripped target values, seed)` (spec 2.7). A value that is not text is as it is, and `task.target_dtype` is still the type as loaded. D48: a text target cell that holds ONLY white space (spaces, tabs; the empty text of a DataFrame cell too) is a missing target, like an empty cell. Its row is dropped and counted in `rows.dropped_missing_target`, by `profile()` and by `stages.usable_rows`, and `stages.decide_task` ignores it. It is not a class of empty text. This is the target only: a feature cell of only white space is still the level of empty text (D42), and a guard of the second pass holds that.

tasks.title: The seed's range
tasks.why_tier: One check on one argument, stated in spec 2.1. It decides no number.
tasks.brief: D45. `seed` is a whole number from 0 to 4,294,967,295 (2**32 - 1). Today any whole number of at least 0 is accepted, and a seed of 2**32, or a timestamp-style seed such as 20261119123456, is refused later by scikit-learn with a raw `InvalidParameterError` from the leak screen's tree, which the command line turns into a traceback and exit 1. Check the upper bound with the other arguments: a seed outside the range is an `InputError` raised before anything is loaded (a table with duplicate column names still gives `InputError`, not `duplicate_columns`), with nothing fitted and nothing written. Do not fold a larger seed down: two seeds would then give one run. The largest allowed seed must run. From the command line it is exit 3 and exactly one line on standard error, `error: input_error: ...`, with no traceback; `--seed` stays an argparse integer and the range is checked by `profile()`. `stages.split_random(n_rows, classes, seed)` takes the same range and raises `InputError` outside it: today it accepts 2**32 and raises a bare `ValueError` for -1 (spec 2.7).

tasks.title: The fast profile's error only when the full profile would run
tasks.why_tier: A clear contract in spec step 7: which named error is raised. It decides no number.
tasks.brief: D46. Under `profile="fast"` with a time column, the row cap can leave too few timestamps to form the holdout and six blocks, and today the run then always stops with `fast_profile_too_few_timestamps`, whose message says to use `profile="full"`. On five dates of 600 rows each the full profile stops too, with `too_few_rows`: the advice is false. Change it as spec step 7 says ('When the fast profile's cap is what left too few timestamps'). When the cap left rows out and the rows kept cannot form the split for want of timestamps (the most recent timestamp alone is over the cap, step 6; or fewer than six timestamps stand before the holdout), work out what step 7 would do with EVERY usable row and the caller's gap, as the full profile would, by calling the same split function. If that split can be formed, raise `FastProfileError` as now. If it cannot, raise the error the full profile would raise there: `too_few_rows`, or `gap_too_large` (nine dates of 450 rows with gap 2). Both places that raise the fast error today follow this rule. One case stays as it is: when the rows kept do hold six timestamps before the holdout and the caller's gap leaves fewer, the error is `gap_too_large`. One test of this file passes today and must go on passing: `test_fast_error_stands_when_the_full_profile_would_run`. So must the first pass's `test_wide_panel_under_fast_raises`.

tasks.title: The console summary prints four significant digits
tasks.why_tier: How numbers that are already computed are printed; the rule is stated in spec 2.2.
tasks.brief: D46. The console summary prints four decimals, so a target on the scale of 1e-4 shows `mse 0.0000 ... baseline 0.0000` and an interval of `0.0000 to 0.0000`, and a p-value of 0.004975 shows as `0.0050`. Print significant digits instead. Every number the summary shows must agree with `profile.json` to four significant digits at any scale, which the spec states as a relative tolerance (spec 2.2): some number printed in the summary, read as a decimal number with its exponent if it has one, is within 0.0005 x |value| of the value. That holds for `score`, `baseline_score` and `skill`, for both ends of both intervals, and for the p-value. A value of exactly zero prints as a zero. The format is yours (six significant digits meets the rule with room to spare), and so are the wording and the layout. A null skill, or a null interval on skill, still needs no number. The second pass's tests of the summary use the older, weaker rule and must stay green: a summary that meets the new rule meets the old one.

tasks.title: The README: which rows the fast profile keeps, and what this pass changed
tasks.why_tier: Prose from known facts.
tasks.brief: The README says of the fast profile that it has 'a cap of 2,000 usable rows (the rows kept are chosen from the seed ...)'. That is true of the random scheme only: under the time-ordered scheme the rows kept are the most recent whole timestamps (spec step 6). Correct it: where the README describes the cap, say both, in your own words. While you are there, bring the README up to date with this pass, briefly and in plain words: `--seed` and `seed` take a whole number from 0 to 4,294,967,295; a target value written with white space round it (`yes `) is read without it, and a target cell of only white space is a missing target; a feature value too large for the models (a magnitude above about 3.4e38) is read as missing and counted with the infinite ones; a regression target with a value too large for squared error stops with the error `non_finite_score`, and no number that is not finite is ever written as null; under the fast profile the error `fast_profile_too_few_timestamps` is raised only when `full` would get past that point; the summary prints significant digits. Every command shown must still work as written, and the README names no file under `verify/` or `tests/`.
